chapter_title: Say the Right Thing (Wit and Humour)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Guests, Manners and First Impressions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.70): paired discussion — meaning of 'Athithi Devo Bhava' and guest courtesy.
Let us read (p.70): choose statements that show polite behaviour towards guests.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick show of hands: who has hosted a guest at home recently? Invite two or three students to name one thing they did to make the guest comfortable, then introduce the play's title and setting in a sentence.

Pairs discuss the two pre-reading prompts under 'Let us read' (p.70): what 'Athithi Devo Bhava' means and why politeness to guests matters. Take brief whole-class responses — note two or three ideas on the board.

Read the five statements about polite guest behaviour (p.70) aloud together. Students decide which ones qualify, then compare choices in their pairs. Discuss the reasoning behind any disagreement as a class.
Wrap up by asking: what one rule of guest behaviour do students think is hardest to follow and why? Collect two or three responses to settle the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading discussion on 'Athithi Devo Bhava' and polite behaviour sets a cultural anchor for Mary's comically failed attempts to follow exactly those norms. A common pitfall here is students listing surface etiquette (offering water, saying please) without engaging with why these acts matter — press for a reason behind each choice. Task on dealing with rude disagreement among friends (p.70, task index 2) is left as self-study; direct students to that page for individual reflection.

periods.activity_title: Reading Scene I: Mrs. Shaw Coaches Mary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.74): complete speaker–words–reason table for Scene I.
Let us discuss (p.74): predict whether Mary can follow her mother's advice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher and volunteer students read Scene I aloud in role — teacher as narrator, students as Mrs. Shaw and Mary (pp.71–74). Pause briefly at stage directions to note what they reveal about mood and tone.

Students work individually to complete the speaker–words–reason table from 'Let us discuss' (p.74), filling in Mary's entries and the missing Mrs. Shaw entry. Share and verify answers in pairs, then briefly with the class.

Whole-class discussion on the prediction question (p.74): do students think Mary will succeed? Invite contrasting views — one for, one against — and ask each side to support their prediction with a detail from Scene I.
Close by asking students to recall, in one sentence, the single most important piece of advice Mrs. Shaw gives Mary. Collect two or three responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Drawing on Scene I's coaching exchange between Mrs. Shaw and Mary, the table task helps students see that dialogue carries both instruction and character — Mrs. Shaw's tone shifts from nurturing to firm. A common pitfall is students copying lines without identifying the speaker's purpose; prompt them to ask 'why does she say this?' for every entry. The Scene I reading aloud also serves as the class text-reading act for Section C.

periods.activity_title: Scene II: Mary's Blunders and Their Consequences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.77): rectify five false statements about Scene II events.
Let us think and reflect (p.79): answer analytical questions on Mary's blunders and the play's theme.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Scene II aloud at a brisk pace (pp.75–77), with students following silently. Pause at each 'no one speaks' stage direction and ask: what would a real room feel like at this moment?

Students work individually on the five rectification statements from 'Let us discuss' (p.77). Pairs compare corrections, then the class settles each item — teacher uses the board to note the corrected facts.

Open discussion on two questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.79): what does the repeated stage direction 'no one speaks' reveal about atmosphere, and what do Mrs. Harding's and Mrs. Lee's restrained responses reveal about their characters? Students respond in turns.
Quick close: one student summarises in a sentence what Mary's inverted goodbye — 'Must you stay? Can't you go?' — tells us about how she handled the visit.

periods.teacher_notes: Scene II is a cascade of identical blunders — each gaffe mirrors the previous one — and students often find it easier to laugh than to analyse. The four remaining analytical questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.79) — on Mary's viewpoint on bankers, her understanding of polite conversation, how her attitude changes, and the play's broader lesson — are rich and worth individual written reflection; direct students to those questions on p.79 as self-study. Watch for students who read the rectification task as a simple factual recall; push them to name what actually happened in the scene, not just negate the false statement.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Manners; Speaking with Stress and Intonation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.84): listen to mother–son manners dialogue; fill blanks choosing correct option.
Let us speak (p.85): speak declarative sentences with falling intonation and word stress.

time_bands.activity: Brief bridge: ask students what clues in a person's voice — not just words — signal whether they are being polite or impatient. Collect two quick responses, then introduce the listening activity.

Teacher reads the mother–son conversation transcript (p.89) aloud at natural pace twice. On first listening students note key manners mentioned; on second they complete the two fill-in-the-blank items from 'Let us listen' (p.84). Check answers briefly as a class.

Introduce falling intonation and sentence stress from 'Let us speak' (p.85). Model the example sentence 'I saw Mrs. Cotter this afternoon' with falling intonation, stressing 'Mrs. Cotter'. Students repeat chorally, then practise the three additional declarative sentences in pairs, taking turns to model and listen.
Cold-call two or three pairs to perform one sentence each. Class listens for correct stress placement and gives a thumbs-up or thumbs-down signal.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.89) features a mother-and-son exchange that parallels Mrs. Shaw and Mary's dynamic — students who have read the play will notice the thematic echo, which reinforces why listening shapes good conversation. A common pitfall in the stress exercise is students placing stress on every content word; model the contrast between stressed and unstressed delivery so they hear the difference clearly. The second listening task (selecting four true statements, p.84) is left as homework reinforcement — assign it only if further listening practice is needed.

periods.activity_title: Rising Intonation and Stress Shifts: Same Words, New Meaning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.85): match each stress-shifted 'I didn't hurt anyone today' to its correct meaning.
Let us speak (p.86): speak the sentence with rising intonation; explain the meaning change.

time_bands.activity: Recap falling intonation from the declarative sentences practised earlier. Ask: what might happen to meaning if the voice rises instead of falls at the sentence's end? Take two guesses.

Display or dictate the five versions of 'I didn't hurt anyone today' (p.85), each stressing a different word. In pairs, students speak each version aloud and match it to the correct meaning from the list (i)–(v). Pairs then share their matches; class settles any disagreements through repeated speaking of the contested version.

Model rising intonation on 'I saw Mrs. Cotter this afternoon' (p.86). Students practise in pairs — one speaks with falling, one with rising intonation — then swap. Each pair explains in one sentence how the meaning shifts between the two versions.
Two or three pairs perform both versions for the class. After each, ask a listener: 'Which version sounded like a question?' Summarise the key takeaway on the board in a single line.

periods.teacher_notes: The five stress-shift variations on one sentence are a powerful demonstration that in English, where you place stress changes what you mean — not just how you sound. Students often treat all five as identical; have them over-exaggerate the stressed word at first so the contrast is audible. The connection to the play is direct: Mary's blunders arise partly from speaking without hearing how her words land on others.

periods.activity_title: Retelling the Play: From Script to Short Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.86): rewrite the play as a short story with character emotions and humour; plan, draft, revise in class.

time_bands.activity: Discuss briefly how a play and a short story differ in format: stage directions become prose description; dialogue becomes narrated speech with said/asked/replied. Model one sentence on the board, converting a stage direction into descriptive prose.

Students plan their story using the five hints from 'Let us write' (p.86): introduction of characters, Mrs. Shaw's coaching, the guests' arrival, key humorous moments, and the ending. They jot a two-line note for each section — teacher circulates to prompt any student stuck on a section.

Students draft their story. Remind them to write in paragraphs, use descriptive language for setting and emotion, and to keep Mary's blunders in sequence. Teacher circulates, offering brief one-line prompts to individuals who stall.

Peer response: partners exchange drafts and underline the single funniest moment they find. Each writer reads their partner's underlined moment aloud, then makes one revision — adding a detail or improving a word — before the sitting closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose retelling of the play is a literary writing task: students must select events, render emotion through narration, and sustain the comic tone of the original. The most common pitfall is students transcribing the dialogue verbatim rather than narrating it — the modelling at the start of the sitting addresses this directly. The full story is planned, drafted, peer-responded and revised within this sitting; no continuation is expected outside it.

periods.activity_title: Suffixes, Confusable Verbs, and Tense in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.80): divide words into root + suffix: gladly, banker, guidance, quietly, walking.
Let us learn (p.81): fill blanks adding suitable suffixes to given root words.
Let us learn (p.82–83): fill blanks using present continuous or present perfect continuous tense.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.81–82): fill blanks with the correct word from confusable verb pairs (fetch/bring, see/look, live/stay, etc.).

time_bands.activity: Introduce suffix word-building using the four examples from 'Let us learn' (p.80): humorous, hilariously, coming, beautiful. Students then divide the five given words — gladly, banker, guidance, quietly, walking — into root + suffix individually. Quick class check on the board.

Students fill in the six blanks in the paragraph (p.81) by adding suitable suffixes to the bracketed root words (effective, wise, discuss, respect, appreciate, response). Pairs compare answers; resolve any dispute by returning to the suffix table established in the first activity.

Introduce the distinction between present continuous and present perfect continuous using the explanation on pp.82–83. Students fill in the seven blanks in the school play preparation paragraph. Teacher writes the first blank on the board as a class exercise, then students complete the rest individually.
Quick round: teacher reads each blank's stem; students call out their answer. Note any split answers and clarify the rule that governs each choice.

periods.teacher_notes: All three tasks draw directly on the play's language: suffixes appear in words like 'quietly' and 'guidance' that occur in the dialogue, and the tense exercise is set in a performance context that echoes the play's own staging. A common pitfall is students guessing the tense by feel rather than applying the has/have + been + -ing rule — insist they identify the signal phrase (for weeks, every day) before choosing. The confusable-verb pairs task (say/tell, fetch/bring, see/look, etc., pp.81–82) is assigned for home reinforcement; the suffix matching table (p.80, task index 1) and sentence-type identification task (p.83, task index 5) are left as self-study reading.

periods.activity_title: Enacting the Play and Exploring Guest Cultures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.86): enact a favourite scene in groups with assigned roles — director, narrator, characters.
Let us explore (p.87): discuss how 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' connects to the play's theme of polite interaction.

time_bands.activity: Form groups of four or five. Each group chooses a scene from 'Say the Right Thing' to enact. Assign roles within the group: director, narrator, and speaking characters. Allow a brief planning moment.

Groups rehearse their scene, incorporating the stage directions printed in brackets in the text (p.86). Teacher moves from group to group, prompting directors to guide expression and narrators to speak stage directions clearly.
Two groups perform their scenes for the class. After each performance, the class offers one observation on what the actors captured well and one suggestion.

Whole-class discussion: unpack 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' — the world is one family (p.87). Students connect the phrase to Mrs. Shaw's message about kindness and politeness to guests, and to Mrs. Harding's and Mrs. Lee's restrained dignity despite Mary's blunders. Conclude with one student's sentence linking the Sanskrit phrase to the play's lesson.

periods.teacher_notes: The enactment task is fully self-contained: groups choose their scene, assign roles, rehearse, and perform within this sitting — no props or preparations from outside the classroom are needed or expected. The 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' discussion deepens the play's theme from a personal etiquette lesson to a broader cultural value, and students who have followed Mary's misadventures are well placed to articulate why listening and empathy are the foundation of that value. The cross-cultural guest-greeting research task (p.87, task index 1) is rich but requires library or internet access; direct students to it as an independent project they can pursue in their own time.

items.item_stem: In Scene I of 'Say the Right Thing', Mrs. Shaw gives Mary several pieces of advice before the guests arrive. Which of the following best describes the main purpose of Mrs. Shaw's coaching?

options.label: A
options.text: To convince Mary to stay in her room while the guests are visiting.

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure Mary memorises exactly what to say so she does not make any mistakes.

options.label: C
options.text: To help Mary develop the social skills needed to hold a polite and pleasant conversation.

options.label: D
options.text: To warn Mary that the guests are wealthy and must be treated with special care.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students choosing this focus on the Hardings' wealth rather than Mrs. Shaw's broader lesson about courtesy and kind conversation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests students misread Mrs. Shaw's advice as scripted lines rather than general principles — she teaches attitudes, not scripts.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Contradicts the play: Mrs. Shaw wants Mary present and participating, not absent.

items.source_lo: Student identifies culturally grounded norms of polite behaviour and predicts character outcomes using dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Pre-reading discussion on 'Athithi Devo Bhava'; selecting polite guest-behaviour statements; Mrs. Shaw's coaching of Mary in Scene I.
items.item_stem: At the end of Scene I, Mary confidently tells her mother she can manage the conversation with the guests. Based on what you have read about Mary's character in Scene I, do you think her confidence is well-founded? Give two reasons from the scene to support your view.

expected_elements: States clearly whether Mary's confidence is well-founded or not.
Cites a detail from Scene I showing Mary resists or misunderstands Mrs. Shaw's advice.
Refers to Mary's impulsive or dismissive responses as evidence she may struggle.
Shows awareness of the gap between Mary's self-belief and her actual readiness.

items.source_context: Scene II blunders — Mrs. Harding's children, the banker, Towzer the dog, inverted goodbye; stage direction 'no one speaks'; guest characters' restrained responses.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Scene II of 'Say the Right Thing'. Identify whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE.
1. Mary congratulates Mrs. Harding on her beautiful children, unaware that Mrs. Harding has no children.
2. Mrs. Lee reveals that her brother is a banker after Mary praises bankers for their sharp thinking.
3. The stage direction 'no one speaks' appears after each of Mary's blunders, signalling the guests' discomfort.
4. Mary correctly delivers the farewell line 'Must you go? Can't you stay?' when the guests prepare to leave.

options.text: Mary congratulates Mrs. Harding on her beautiful children, unaware that Mrs. Harding has no children.
Mary correctly delivers the farewell line 'Must you go? Can't you stay?' when the guests prepare to leave.
Mrs. Lee reveals that her brother is a banker after Mary praises bankers for their sharp thinking.
The stage direction 'no one speaks' appears after each of Mary's blunders, signalling the guests' discomfort.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Mary assumes Mrs. Harding has children and compliments them, but Mrs. Harding has none.
2. False — Mary dismisses bankers as unable to think; it is then that Mrs. Lee reveals her brother is a banker.
3. True — the stage direction 'no one speaks' recurs after each of Mary's social blunders, capturing the awkward silence.
4. False — Mary inverts the line entirely, saying 'Must you stay? Can't you go?' instead of the polite farewell her mother taught her.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character behaviour, dramatic irony, and thematic meaning using a humorous dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Scene II blunders — Mrs. Harding's children, the banker, Towzer the dog, inverted goodbye; stage direction 'no one speaks'; guest characters' restrained responses.
items.item_stem: Throughout Scene II, Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee respond to Mary's blunders with quiet corrections rather than open anger. What does their restrained behaviour reveal about their characters, and what does the playwright achieve by giving them these responses rather than making them react with outrage?

expected_elements: Describes Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee as dignified or self-controlled characters.
Notes that quiet correction keeps the comedy gentle rather than confrontational.
Explains how restraint makes each blunder funnier by highlighting Mary's obliviousness.
Connects the guests' manner to the play's theme that true politeness is gracious, not aggressive.

items.item_stem: In the mother–son conversation about manners, the mother asks her son what he should do when someone else is speaking. Which of the following best captures the son's response and the manner in which the mother receives it?

options.label: A
options.text: The son is unsure and says nothing; the mother provides the answer herself.

options.label: B
options.text: The son says they should raise their hand and ask permission; the mother suggests a different approach.

options.label: C
options.text: The son says they should speak louder so everyone can hear; the mother gently corrects him.

options.label: D
options.text: The son says they should wait for their turn and not interrupt; the mother confirms this is correct.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have confused the 'inside voice' exchange with the turn-taking exchange — both concern voice or speech behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is importing a classroom convention not present in the transcript.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have remembered that the son sometimes hesitates but confused hesitation with silence on this specific point.

items.item_stem: The mother in the conversation uses the grocery queue incident, the bumping-into-a-lady episode, and the library example as teaching moments. What does her choice of everyday situations — rather than formal rules — suggest about how she believes good manners are best learned? Support your answer with a detail from the conversation.

expected_elements: States that the mother believes manners are learned through real, lived experience.
Notes she links each rule to a specific moment the son actually experienced.
Cites one example — grocery queue, apology to the lady, or library voice.
Infers that experiential teaching helps the son understand the reason behind each manner, not just the rule.

items.item_stem:
Choose the sentence from the list below and read it aloud twice — first with falling intonation, then with rising intonation. After each reading, tell your listener in one sentence what the difference in meaning is.
Sentence: 'You always talk too much.'

expected_elements: Demonstrates clearly audible falling intonation on the first reading.
Demonstrates clearly audible rising intonation on the second reading.
States that falling intonation makes it a firm statement; rising makes it sound uncertain or questioning.
Uses natural pace and appropriate stress on 'always' or 'talk'.

items.source_context: Falling and rising intonation on declarative sentences from the play; five stress-shift versions of 'I didn't hurt anyone today'; meaning changes through intonation.
items.item_stem: Work in pairs. One student plays Mary, the other plays Mrs. Shaw. Mary must deliver the line 'I didn't hurt anyone today' twice — once stressing the word 'I' and once stressing the word 'hurt'. After each delivery, Mrs. Shaw responds with one sentence explaining what she understood Mary to mean. Then swap roles and repeat.

expected_elements: Mary produces noticeably different stress placement in each of the two deliveries.
Mrs. Shaw's response correctly reflects the meaning shift — 'I specifically' versus 'did not cause harm'.
Both students switch roles and maintain the distinction in the second round.
Delivery uses natural speed and volume; stress is not exaggerated to the point of parody.

items.item_stem: Write a single paragraph (7–10 sentences) that narrates the moment the guests arrive in 'Say the Right Thing' and describes Mary's first blunder. Write in the third person, use at least one adverb to show how Mary speaks, and include one sentence that conveys Mrs. Shaw's reaction.

expected_elements: Third-person narration sustained throughout the paragraph.
Accurately depicts Mary's blunder about Mrs. Harding's children.
Includes at least one adverb of manner to describe Mary's speech.
Contains a sentence conveying Mrs. Shaw's embarrassment or alarm.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Mary, writing in your diary the evening after Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee's visit. In your entry, reflect on at least two of the blunders you made, explain what you should have said or done instead, and share what you feel about the way the visit ended with your inverted goodbye. Write 100–120 words in first person.

expected_elements: First-person diary voice maintained throughout; includes a date or salutation.
Accurately references at least two of Mary's blunders from the play.
Reflects on what Mary should have said or done differently in each case.
Responds to the inverted farewell with honest emotion — embarrassment, humour, or resolve to improve.

items.item_stem: Match each word from the play in Column A with its correct analysis in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
gladly|glad + -ly (root + adverb suffix)
banker|bank + -er (root + agent suffix)
guidance|guide + -ance (root + noun suffix)
quietly|quiet + -ly (root + adverb suffix)
walking|walk + -ing (root + present participle suffix)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d, 5-e (using the order of Column A entries: gladly → glad + -ly; banker → bank + -er; guidance → guide + -ance; quietly → quiet + -ly; walking → walk + -ing).

items.item_stem:
Read the two sentences below and fill in the blanks with the correct tense form of the verb given in brackets — either present continuous or present perfect continuous.
(i) Mrs. Shaw _______ (prepare) the sitting room for the past hour before the guests arrive.
(ii) Right now, Mary _______ (talk) to Mrs. Harding about the neighbours, and her mother looks worried.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) has been preparing — the action started in the past and continues up to now, shown by 'for the past hour'. (ii) is talking — the action is happening at this exact moment, shown by 'right now'.

items.item_stem: Your group is planning to enact the scene in which Mary makes her most memorable blunder — congratulating Mrs. Harding on her beautiful children. Write a brief director's note (4–6 sentences) for the student playing Mary, explaining how Mary should move, speak, and react when Mrs. Harding corrects her, so that the scene is both funny and true to the character.

expected_elements: Advises on Mary's tone — confident and cheerful before the correction.
Describes a visible physical or vocal reaction when Mrs. Harding reveals she has no children.
Keeps the humour gentle, not mocking — the blunder is Mary's, not Mrs. Harding's.
Shows awareness of stage directions or silences noted in the play's text.

items.item_stem: The Sanskrit phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' means 'the world is one family'. Write a short response (one paragraph, 80–100 words) explaining how this idea connects to the way Mrs. Shaw tries to prepare Mary for the visit, and why Mary's behaviour in Scene II falls short of this ideal. Use at least one specific example from the play.

expected_elements: Explains 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' as treating all people — including guests — as family.
Links Mrs. Shaw's coaching to the idea that kindness and respect extend beyond one's own household.
Cites a specific blunder where Mary treats guests as outsiders rather than with familial warmth.
Concludes that the play shows polite conversation as a practice of that inclusive ideal.
